prompt: When should a cell in a quilted system ask the JEV oracle (an external judge) versus compute the answer locally from its neighbors? Design the decision rule, name its failure mode, and say how the ledger catches it.
seed_ignore_finding: deepseek endpoint ignores `seed` (probe receipted); diversity enforced via lenses; seeds are book-keeping

an engineer who wants the smallest mechanism that could work
a teacher who explains by building one small piece at a time

steps.text: The quilted system consists of cells communicating with neighbors, a JEV oracle, and a public ledger.
Each cell can compute a local confidence value C from signed neighbor messages and obtain the oracle’s authoritative value if requested.
A cell must query the JEV only when C < T (a protocol‑defined threshold); otherwise it accepts the local value.
C is verifiable because it is derived from signed messages; T is fixed in the protocol, preventing manipulation.
If a cell claims C ≥ T while in fact C < T, it may avoid an oracle request for malicious gain.
The ledger records the necessary neighbor signatures when C ≥ T; absence or invalid signatures on the ledger prove a false threshold claim.
Thus the ledger audit trail detects the false‑confidence failure, ensuring only legitimate oracle consultations occur.

steps.text: The engineer wants the minimal decision rule for oracle queries in a quilted system.
Local computation is cheap, but if neighbors disagree, a local view may be unreliable.
Rule: a cell queries the JEV oracle only when its local result differs from the majority of neighbor outputs.
Failure mode: a colluding cluster of corrupt neighbors outputs the same false value so no disagreement occurs, called the Silent Cartel.
The ledger cannot detect silent cartels by looking only at local consistency.
Catch: the ledger performs a deterministic random audit—using the current block hash to select a small fraction of cells to verify via JEV regardless of local agreement—breaking any silent cartel.

steps.text: A quilted system consists of many cells connected to their neighbors and an external JEV oracle that can be queried for ground truth.
In a distributed setting local computation (from neighbors) is cheap but may be misled by colluding neighbors, while oracle queries are costly but reliable.
Thus a cell should only query the oracle when local evidence is ambiguous or insufficient to guarantee correctness.
Rule: If the maximum disagreement between a cell’s neighbors exceeds threshold T or the cell cannot resolve a deterministic transition from its visible state, then ask the JEV oracle.
Failure mode: Colluding neighbors suppress neighbor disagreement so that cells avoid oracle queries, creating silent false consensus.
Ledger catches this by requiring a signed proof of oracle query whenever a cell’s state diverges from the local majority; random audits trigger oracle queries to verify disputed cells.
This rule, failure naming, and ledger check together enforce correct local inference while penalizing oracle avoidance.
